entries.gave: Read the Cut with its six decisions and no More, the stub README, pyproject.toml, the invoicer code and tests, the design tree and the earlier README records. The people: accounting colleagues on Windows laptops with Microsoft 365 Excel, who save an invoice lines from Excel and print the invoice at the client rate in PowerShell with no Python; and the developer who does the one-time pipx setup on each accounting machine and checks that it works.
Read readme best-practice.md with template.md, and refactor-doc best-practice.md, to their end before any change.

No product vision file; the Cut and the design tree name the role: a colleague from accounting who keeps an invoice lines in Excel and prints invoices for clients, and writes no Python; plus the developer of the one-time setup.
The end they reach: print each client invoice at that client tax rate yourself, without asking a developer, from the goal.
The one thing it gives, in accounting words: it prints the invoice of the rows you save from Excel, with subtotal, tax and total at the rate you type.
Read pyproject.toml to its end: invoicer 1.5.0, requires-python >=3.9, script invoicer = invoicer.command:main, no license field.
The kind: a command that you type in PowerShell, the word accounting meets in the steps.

Products of the kind, invoice generators from CSV such as invoice-generator CLIs and spreadsheet invoice templates, give a PDF or a page to print, a currency, the client name, an invoice number and date, and a tax rate per line.
The benefit, a printed invoice, leads a reader to expect a paper or PDF invoice with their client details on it.
The issue tracker of lovaizu/playground holds no wontfix request about invoicer; its issues are the goals of this work.
In command.py and render.py: it prints text to the PowerShell window, no PDF; every amount in EUR, with no option to change it; no client name, number or date; one --rate for all lines. Each not met.
Each of the four would turn a reader against it: a client billed in another currency, an invoice that needs number and date, a PDF, mixed tax rates. All four kept.

No product vision; the person signed off invoicer as it stands, printing text in EUR at one rate with no client details, and the plan, so these are settled as the signed-off product, not asked; each goes in the Made settled for the person to sign off.
All four kept for Non-goals; none moves to a status.
Version 1.5.0 in pyproject.toml, above 1.0.
The use toward the goal, a run of invoicer on saved lines, is tried in step 5 by pipx install and runs at two rates; tests/test_command.py covers it, and the person signed invoicer off.
The repository lovaizu/playground is public, not archived, and kept by the developers.
Ready: 1.5.0, the use works, kept up; the README has no status line.
The repository holds no license file, and the GitHub API gives license null; by the Cut decision on N4 the person leaves the license out of this pull request.
No SPDX identifier to name: the Cut decision says the README names no license.
No copied work of others in the repository: invoicer uses only the Python standard library.
The use: a colleague from accounting prints one client invoice from rows saved in Excel, the goal.
The task, per the Cut decision on N6: three rows, Design 100.00 x 2, Hosting 10.50 x 1, Discount -20.00 x 1, saved as lines.csv, printed at 19 and at 7.7 percent.
How well: the invoice text as printed, its tax changing with the rate typed; how fast: the one command line typed, no Python.
The cut: the Excel rows, the Excel save steps, the command typed and the full invoice printed at each rate; nothing cut, as the command prints no progress lines.
No product vision; the one way, from the goal and the signed-off command: you type the client tax rate on each run, and it turns the saved rows into the invoice at that rate.
The problem today, in accounting words: I have to ask a developer each time I need an invoice at a client rate.
Doubts: are the totals right to the cent; what if I make a mistake in a row or the rate; will my Excel save the file the way it reads it.
The issues of lovaizu/playground hold the goal texts of this work, which raise the same: a rate per client, no Python, no developer to ask; nothing new added.
Kept three: totals to the cent, a mistake in a row or rate, Excel separators; the walkthrough settles the rate per client, so that one is not a heading of its own.

Ideas that answer them, from the signed-off command: each amount rounded half up to the cent and the subtotal the sum of the printed amounts; a wrong row or rate refused with nothing printed and the row named; rows read as CSV with semicolons and a decimal point.
None missing: each doubt has its part in the code.
No idea that matters to the users is missing; nothing to ask.
No way to make it work is missing; no requirement handed back.
From pyproject.toml: Python 3.9 or later, no other package; the install is pipx install of the repository, which is public, so its main.zip URL needs no Git; the script invoicer.

On an empty Windows laptop: Python from python.org with its py launcher; pipx, installed by py -m pip; an internet connection; and signing in as the accounting colleague, as pipx installs the command for one Windows account.
Checks: whoami shows the colleague account; py --version shows Python 3.9 or later; and after the install, invoicer --help in a new PowerShell window prints its usage line.
No docs folder or changelog; pyproject.toml names no URL; the repository lovaizu/playground has issues on.
Kept: the issues, for the developers to report a fault or ask for a change; invoicer --help shows the options, given in Installation.
Help has a place, the issues; nothing to ask.
Read README.md to its end: a two-line stub, a heading Playground and one sentence, for no reader of invoicer.

Readers, from the Cut decision on N1: a colleague from accounting who wants an invoice printed at a client rate; the developer who sets invoicer up once on an accounting laptop and wants to see it work.
Accounting knows Excel, Save As and client tax rates, and not PowerShell, CSV separators or Python; the developer knows Python and pipx, and not the accounting laptops.
Sections by purpose: Requirements and Installation for the developer alone; Walkthrough for accounting, the everyday steps; How it works for both; the template sections hold one topic each.
Each doubt that accounting looks for gets its own heading under How it works; the template sets the other headings.
Forms: the install commands and the everyday steps as numbered steps and code blocks; Non-goals and Requirements as bulleted lists; the mechanism as an SVG figure; each doubt answer as prose.

Words of the readers: Excel names File, Options, Advanced, Use system separators, Decimal separator, Save As and CSV UTF-8 (Comma delimited); Windows names Open in Terminal and PowerShell; the person writes tax rate, line, row, invoice.
Chosen: row for an Excel row, line for a line of the invoice, tax rate, PowerShell; CSV written out as comma-separated values where first met; pipx kept for the developer, who knows it.
Facts in more than one place: the form of a row, which --help and the walkthrough both show; the usage line, which --help prints.
The form of a row is stated in full in the Walkthrough, where accounting looks for it; the options stay with invoicer --help, which Installation names as the sign.
No two places state a fact differently; nothing to ask.
Names in play: the file of rows as lines.csv; the command as invoicer; the rate as tax rate; Excel rows and invoice lines.
One name each: lines.csv for the saved file, invoicer in code format for the command, tax rate for the rate.
Row is kept for an Excel row, as the command messages say row 2; line is kept for a line of the invoice.

Took the six Cut decisions as they stand: no License section and no LICENSE file; the developer pipx setup on Windows with invoicer --help as the check; accounting everyday steps in Excel and PowerShell in the Walkthrough, with the decimal point set in Excel Options; a run at 19 and 7.7 percent. Settled: install from the public main.zip URL so no Git is needed; sign in as the colleague, as pipx installs for one account; Non-goals PDF, currency EUR only, no client details, one rate per invoice; help in the repository issues. No asks.

Wrote the opening by the template: invoicer is a PowerShell command that prints an invoice from rows saved in Excel, at the tax rate you type; for you when you work in accounting and bill clients from invoice lines in Excel; you print each invoice at the client rate yourself, without a developer or Python.
Took out each of the three sentences in turn: each one alone says what, who for, or what they achieve, so none deleted; no status sentence, as it is ready.
No vague or praising word in the opening.
Read as a developer who bills no one: work in accounting and bill clients from invoice lines kept in Excel tells them it is not theirs to use day to day; kept.
Non-goals lists four: no PDF, no client name, number or date, EUR only, one tax rate for the whole invoice.
The PDF item says the text can be copied into the letter, and the details item says it prints the lines and totals; the others have no other way.
Ready, so no status line at the top.
No License section written, by the Cut decision on N4: the README names no license; rn template check asks for the section, a conflict handed back.
No license link to follow, as the README names none; no LICENSE file added.
Sections in the template order: opening, Non-goals, Requirements, Installation, Walkthrough, How it works, Documentation; License left out by the Cut decision.
Within the Walkthrough, the once-only Excel setting comes before the steps for each invoice; within Requirements, who does the setup comes first.

Read README.md from the top as a colleague from accounting: after the opening, what does it not do; after Non-goals, who sets it up, which Requirements answers; after Installation, how do I print one, which the Walkthrough answers; after it, can I trust the totals and what if I mistype, which How it works answers.
No answer stands before its question; nothing moved.
Each next section answers the question written; the first requirement names the developer, so accounting knows the setup is not theirs.

Ran the task in a throwaway copy with an empty home: pipx install of the repository, lines.csv with a byte order mark and CRLF rows as Excel saves it, invoicer lines.csv --rate 19 and --rate 7.7, each exit 0; outputs kept as they came.
Wrote the rows as an Excel table of columns A to C, and each command with its invoice as a console code block, with the PowerShell prompt PS>.
The Walkthrough opens with the result: the client invoice in PowerShell, with the tax at the rate typed.
A newcomer from accounting can say: I save my rows as lines.csv, type invoicer with the client rate, and get the invoice, tax 36.20 at 19% and 14.67 at 7.7% for the same rows.
The one way in one sentence: You type each client tax rate, and invoicer turns your saved rows into the invoice at that rate.
That sentence stands first in How it works, before the figure and the three answers.
A newcomer reading only it can say back: I give the rate each time and it makes the invoice from my rows.

The mechanism below the one way: lines.csv from Excel, read row by row, each amount to the cent and the tax at the typed rate, the invoice in PowerShell; each answer says which of these parts answers it.
Drew images/how-it-works.svg: the four parts as one flow, the --rate input into the amounts, and each of the three doubts beside the part that answers it, with what the reader gets.
Labels in accounting words: lines.csv saved from Excel, reads each row, amounts to the cent, the invoice in PowerShell, the client tax rate.
The only own name is --rate, explained in the figure as the client tax rate typed on each run.
A newcomer can say back: it rounds each line to the cent so the totals add up, refuses a wrong row or rate by naming it, and reads Excel semicolons.
Installation holds the three commands to copy: py -m pip install --user pipx, py -m pipx ensurepath, py -m pipx install of the main.zip URL.
The steps end with the sign: in a new PowerShell window, invoicer --help prints its usage line, quoted.

Ran the three install steps in a throwaway copy with an empty home, on Linux, as no Windows machine is at hand: python3 for py, --break-system-packages that Debian alone needs, and the pushed branch zip for main.zip, as main lacks the command until merge; each exit 0, and a new shell printed usage: invoicer [-h] --rate PERCENT LINES. The Windows py launcher, PowerShell and Excel steps stay untried.
Documentation gives one link, the issues of lovaizu/playground by URL, for the developers to report a fault or ask for a change.
The issues URL opens the issue list of lovaizu/playground, has_issues true by the GitHub API; images/how-it-works.svg opens from the README folder.
Headings are fixed by the readme template; the doubt headings start with the reader question words, such as What if a row or the tax rate is wrong?

Each first sentence says what the section gives: the first requirement names the developer who sets it up, the Walkthrough opens with the invoice you have at the end, each doubt opens with what invoicer does.
Read headings and first sentences for each purpose: accounting finds the Walkthrough and skips Requirements by its developer line; the developer finds Requirements and Installation.
Each sentence serves accounting or the developer; none marked.
No sentence marked, so no other document sought.
Nothing moved.
Nothing to ask about.
The stub sentence about the Playground went, as it serves no reader of invoicer.
Cut words: of its own in the row step, so that sentences stay at 20 words or fewer.
Articles and that kept throughout.

Read README.md again from the top as each reader: accounting still finds the column order, no heading row, the save type and file name, and the command; the developer finds the account, Python, commands and sign.
The once-only Excel setting stands before the save step that needs it; lines.csv is named in the save step before the command uses it.
Outside facts linked: python.org for Python, the issues by URL; Excel and Windows menu names spelled out.
Sentences start from the known, such as Excel separates the cells with the list separator of Windows, which is ; for euro formats.
Conditions first: If invoicer says that a row has 1 field, set List separator; In a new PowerShell window, invoicer --help prints.
The exception to the price rule, a discount as a negative price, follows the row rule in the next step.
Read README.md from the top: no place needed a look back or ahead.
Wrote the Excel setting and the steps for each invoice as numbered lists, the rows as a table, Non-goals and Requirements as bulleted lists.
No sequence between parties to draw; no Mermaid diagram.
The mechanism, its parts and what passes between them, drawn as images/how-it-works.svg with its layout set.
Split the cent answer into one point each: the subtotal adds up the printed amounts, each rounded half up; the tax is rounded too, so the amounts add up to the total.
Actors as subjects: invoicer prints, Excel separates the cells, pipx installs, you type; the steps are imperatives addressed to the reader.
Replaced Fix it in Excel with Fix the row in Excel, as it could mean the row or the tax rate.
No noun made from a verb left, such as installation outside its template heading.
Objects next to their verbs, such as Set Decimal separator to a point, Name the file lines.csv.
Read README.md to its end word by word: each sentence reads one way; the menu paths are bold names joined by >.
Each word is the chosen one: row for an Excel row, line for a line of the invoice, tax rate throughout, the Excel and Windows menu names as they show them.
No term of the team to define: pipx stays for the developer, who knows it, and --rate is explained in the figure.

CSV stands only inside the Excel type name CSV UTF-8 (Comma delimited), which accounting picks as Excel shows it, so it is not written out, unlike the plan in N6.2; PDF and EUR are the words accounting uses.
The form of a row is stated in full once, in the Walkthrough steps 1 and 2, with the table showing it.
The options are not repeated: Installation names invoicer --help, which shows them.
Each kept name written the same way: invoicer in code format, lines.csv in code format, tax rate in lowercase.

Made README.md by the readme template, with images/how-it-works.svg: opening, four Non-goals, Requirements and Installation for the developer pipx setup on Windows ending in invoicer --help, the Walkthrough with the once-only Excel decimal point setting, the steps to save lines.csv as CSV UTF-8 and run invoicer in PowerShell, and the run at 19 and 7.7 percent, three doubts in How it works, the issues in Documentation; no License section, by the Cut decision.

Tried in a throwaway copy with an empty home, on Linux: the pip, ensurepath and pipx install steps exit 0, and a new shell prints the usage line the README quotes; lines.csv with a byte order mark and CRLF rows, as Excel saves CSV UTF-8, prints at 19 and 7.7 percent exactly the invoices the Walkthrough shows; a comma-separated row is refused as row 1 with 1 field, as How it works says. Untried, as no Windows machine is at hand: the py launcher, PowerShell, Open in Terminal and the Excel menus.

Wrote the Made in rounds/README.md/1/made.json: where each of the six Cut decisions lands, and six points settled with their grounds: the main.zip URL, the colleague Windows account, the four Non-goals, Open in Terminal, the three doubts, help in the issues.
rn check of done: shortened the opening sentence to 20 words; it still says README.md lacks the template section ## License, which the Cut decision on N4 rules out, so the generator ends lacks.
